academicTalks.transcript: Today, let’s look at how mangrove trees survive along tropical coasts. Their roots grow in muddy shorelines where saltwater rises and falls with the tides. Most plants would lose too much water in such salty soil, but mangroves use several strategies. First, some species block much of the salt before it enters their roots. Others take in salt but store it in old leaves, which later fall off. Mangroves also have unusual aerial roots that rise above the mud. At low tide, tiny pores in these roots absorb oxygen from the air, because waterlogged mud contains very little oxygen. These adaptations do more than help individual trees survive. Dense root systems slow waves and hold sediment in place, reducing coastal erosion. The roots also create sheltered spaces where young fish and crabs can hide from larger animals. For that reason, when mangrove forests are cleared, nearby fishing communities may lose both shoreline protection and nursery habitat for seafood species. So mangroves are not simply trees growing near the ocean; they are living systems that connect plant survival, animal populations, and coastal stability.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the talk?

options.text: To describe methods for tracking tides beside tropical shorelines
To compare tropical fishing methods and their effects in several regions
To show why saltwater prevents every coastal tree from growing
To explain mangrove adaptations and their value to coastal ecosystems

questions.explanationZh: 主旨是紅樹林的存活策略及其保護海岸、提供棲地的作用，呼應「connect plant survival」。捕魚方法、測潮與無法耐鹽皆非主旨。

To release excess salt when ocean water reaches the roots
To absorb oxygen from the air when the tide is low

academicTalks.transcript:
Today I’d like to introduce thermal conductivity, which is simply how readily heat moves through a material. Imagine placing one end of a metal spoon in hot soup. Before long, the handle feels warm because energy travels through the spoon. In metals, tiny charged particles called electrons can move freely and carry energy quickly. That is why a copper pan heats more evenly than a wooden spoon.

Wood and foam contain many small pockets of air. Air does not transfer heat efficiently, so those pockets slow the movement of energy. Materials that slow heat transfer are called insulators. Winter jackets use this idea: their fluffy filling traps air near the body and reduces heat loss.

Engineers choose materials by considering both conductivity and purpose. A cooking-pot base should conduct heat well, but its handle should be insulated so a cook can hold it safely. The same principle helps architects select wall materials that keep buildings comfortable while reducing the energy needed for heating or cooling. So, thermal conductivity is not just a laboratory measurement; it affects ordinary objects and larger designs alike.

academicTalks.transcript: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many towns in the United States established free public libraries. Earlier libraries often charged subscriptions, meaning users paid a fee to borrow books. Reform advocates wanted a different model: libraries supported by local taxes and open to all residents. They argued that literacy, the ability to read and write, served democracy. A voter who could read newspapers, compare arguments, and find information could participate more fully in public life. Tax funding also made it possible for a library to buy books for children and workers who could not afford private collections. Not everyone approved. Some residents objected to paying taxes for books they might never borrow. Private booksellers worried that free lending would reduce sales. Supporters answered that libraries did not simply replace stores; they provided shared access to information and often encouraged new readers to buy books later. The debate shows that a public library was not viewed only as a building. It was a proposal about who should pay for knowledge and who should be able to use it.

questions.stem: How did the proposed public-library model differ from earlier libraries?

options.text: It charged residents a subscription to borrow books.
It used local taxes and served all residents.
It depended on private booksellers to lend books.
It limited borrowing to children and workers.

options.text: Children could replace school lessons with library books.

questions.explanationZh: 倡議者說能讀報、比較論點並查找資訊的人可「participate more fully in public life」。其餘皆非原文提出的民主理由。

It concerned access to knowledge and its public funding.

academicTalks.transcript: Today, let's look at why a small price change can sometimes produce a large change in sales. Economists call this price elasticity of demand. It measures how sensitive buyers are to a change in price. Suppose a campus café raises the price of its reusable water bottle from ten dollars to twelve. If students can easily buy similar bottles elsewhere, many may switch stores. Demand is elastic, meaning sales respond strongly to price. But imagine the café sells a textbook required for one course and available nowhere else on campus. A small price increase may reduce sales very little. That demand is inelastic because buyers have few alternatives. Time also matters. Right before classes begin, students may need the textbook immediately. Later, they can search online or borrow a copy, so demand can become more elastic. Businesses use this idea when setting prices. They do not simply ask, "Will customers dislike a higher price?" They ask whether the extra money earned per item will be greater than the money lost when fewer items are sold. The answer depends on available substitutes, how necessary the product is, and how much time buyers have to adjust.

options.text: To argue that price increases always reduce profits
To explain why demand reacts differently to price changes
To describe how cafés choose reusable products
To compare textbook costs at several universities

questions.explanationZh: 教授用水瓶與課本說明價格彈性：需求對價格變動的反應不同。其他選項分別縮小成成本、產品或錯稱一定虧損，非講題重點。
